newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: Ariane rocket puts two satellites in orbit.
newsitem.headline: Ariane rocket puts two satellites in orbit.

text.p: Western Europe's 97th Ariane rocket placed two satellites in orbit after a launch from equatorial French Guiana late on Tuesday.

The Ariane 44L, equipped with four liquid strap-on boosters -- the most powerful in the Ariane rocket series -- lifted off into a cloudy night sky at 8.20 p.m. local time (2320 GMT) from the European Space Agency (ESA) launch center in Kourou, French Guiana on the northeast coast of South America.
Twenty-one minutes after takeoff, space officials said the INMARSAT-2F4 satellite separated from the rocket.

The London-based International Maritime Satellite Organization (INMARSAT) said the 2 ton satellite will provide mobile satellite communications in the Atlantic ocean region for ships, trucks and aircraft using terminals the size of laptop computers.
"We (INMARSAT) have our roots in maritime but we have progressed a long way," Warren Grace, INMARSAT director general told a pre-launch news conference.
"We've spread into aeronautical and land-mobile and now have global coverage," he said.

Grace said the cost of INMARSAT-2F4 -- satellite, launch and insurance was more than $160 million. The satellite was built in the U.S. by Lockheed Martin and is designed to operate in space for 13 years.
Five minutes later the INSAT-2A satellite separated from the Ariane rocket.
The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) said the 2.1 ton satellite will provide telecommunications throughout India and neigboring countries.
ISRO chairman Krishnaswamy Kasturirangan said the Indian-built INSAT-2A cost considerably less than a comparable satellite manufactured in the West.
"If we had to go to the U.S. or Europe to buy this class of satellite we would have to pay another 25 to 30 percent more," he said
ISRO said the insured value of their mission was more than $100 million and the launch cost exceeded the cost of the satellite.
Tuesday's Ariane mission, the 97th, precedes the 96th Ariane mission that was scheduled for launch last month but scrubbed because of problems in that rocket's satellite payload.
The Paris-based Arianespace company that launches the Ariane-4 rocket series has led the commercial rocket launch market for over a decade, capturing over half of the world's market.
The company has successfully placed 130 heavy satellites into orbit since 1981 and said it has firm orders to launch 39 satellites worth an estimated $3.3 billion.

It fears, however, its lead is threatened by American consolidation -- notably the merger of Lockheed and Martin Marrietta and the planned purchase of McDonnell Douglas Corp. by Boeing late this year.
The first more powerful, new generation Ariane-5 rocket exploded 37 seconds after its maiden launch in June 1996 in a major setback for the European Space program.

Arianespace was scheduled to take over operations of Ariane-5 early this year, but the new rocket's commercial future is in doubt and a second experimental launch of the more powerful rocket is planned for September at the earliest.
